meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What matters is precisely this, the unspoken at the edge of the spoken'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Woolf: it is a reworded line from Eavan Boland's 1997 essay "Letter to a Young Woman Poet". The Woolf diary entry it's credited to doesn't exist.

answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — actually Eavan Boland
answer.sourceLine: The words come from Boland’s essay “Letter to a Young Woman Poet” (1997), later collected in A Journey with Two Maps (2011). She wrote “what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken.” The popular “What matters is precisely this” is a reworded version, and the Woolf diary entry it is usually credited to does not exist.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Letter to a Young Woman Poet
PN Review 118 (vol. 24, no. 2), Nov–Dec 1997; collected in A Journey with Two Maps (W. W. Norton, 2011)
Credited to Woolf’s diary for 21 July 1912. No such entry exists.

source.excerpt: …presence shapes what I am saying. And so in the last light, at the end of the day, what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken. And so I have made a fiction…
trail: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ lists the line under misattributions. It notes that the line is credited to Woolf’s diary for 21 July 1912, “but there is no entry for that date or even for that year,” and names Eavan Boland as the source.
Boland’s essay “Letter to a Young Woman Poet” appeared in PN Review 118 (November–December 1997) ↗.

The essay is collected in Boland’s A Journey with Two Maps: Becoming a Woman Poet (W. W. Norton, 2011) ↗. The Internet Archive’s full-text index finds the passage “what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken” in it.
The misattribution still circulates. In a 2023 BOMB interview ↗, a poet describes moments that intimate, “as Woolf would say, ‘the unspoken at the edge of the spoken.’”
source.excerptNote: This is the passage as it appears in the Internet Archive full-text index of three printed editions: By Herself (Graywolf, 2000), Word: On Being a [Woman] Writer (Feminist Press, 2004) and A Journey with Two Maps (Norton, 2011). The viral version replaces Boland’s “what matters is language. Is” with “What matters is precisely this,” and leaves out the reference to language.

source.rightsNote: The words are Eavan Boland’s, from “Letter to a Young Woman Poet.” The essay was copyrighted in 1997 and collected in A Journey with Two Maps (2011). Any work first published in 1931 or later is still in copyright in the US, so this essay is in copyright. It is not a public-domain Woolf text.

author.name: Eavan Boland
author.heading: About the real author
author.bio: Eavan Boland (1944–2020) was an Irish poet and essayist, born and died in Dublin. From 1996 she was a tenured professor of English at Stanford University, where she directed the creative writing program. Her prose collection A Journey with Two Maps: Becoming a Woman Poet (2011) ends with “Letter to a Young Woman Poet,” the essay this line is taken from.

copyAttribution: "At the end of the day, what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken." — Eavan Boland, "Letter to a Young Woman Poet" (1997). Often misattributed to Virginia Woolf.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Woolf
misattribution.intro: The fragment sounds like Woolf: it is lyrical, it is about silence, and it is short enough to share. Online it usually comes with a precise-looking diary date. That date turns out to be invented.

items.why: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ reports that Woolf’s diary has no entry for that date or for that year, and puts the line among its misattributions.

Boland’s text, as indexed in A Journey with Two Maps ↗, reads “what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken.” The popular version swaps in “precisely this” and drops the word “language,” which is the subject of Boland’s sentence.
A 2023 BOMB interview ↗ credits the phrase to Woolf (“as Woolf would say”), showing that the misattribution has reached literary publications.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Eavan Boland’s, from “Letter to a Young Woman Poet” (1997): “what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken.” See the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗.

context.heading: What Boland was saying
lead: “Letter to a Young Woman Poet” is addressed to an imagined poet of the future. It opens: “I wish I knew you.” Near its close Boland says that what matters “in the last light, at the end of the day” is language, and she describes language as “the unspoken at the edge of the spoken.”
Without the word “language,” the viral version becomes a general remark about silence. Its rhythm also sounds like Woolf, which helps explain how it came to carry her name and an invented diary date.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain lists the line as a misattribution: it is credited to Woolf's Diary for 21 July 1912, but there is no entry for that date or year, and the source is Eavan Boland ('at the end of the day, what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken', A Journey with Two Maps).
'Letter to a Young Woman Poet' by Eavan Boland appeared in PN Review 118, Vol. 24 No. 2, November-December 1997, and opens 'I wish I knew you.'
PN Review's contributor page lists 'Article in PN Review 118 (1997) Letter to a Young Woman Poet' by Eavan Boland.

The Internet Archive item is Boland's A Journey with Two Maps: Becoming a Woman Poet (W.W. Norton, 2011). IA full-text search returns 'in the last light, at the end of the day, what matters is language. Is the unspoken at the edge of the spoken. And so I have made a fiction' from it.
By Herself: Women Reclaim Poetry (Graywolf, 2000) reprints Boland's 'Letter to a Young Woman Poet', credited 'copyright © 1997 by Eavan Boland', and IA full-text search finds the passage in it.
A 2023 BOMB interview with Maya C. Popa attributes 'the unspoken at the edge of the spoken' to Woolf ('as Woolf would say').
Wikiquote's Virginia Woolf page does not list this line and points to the Virginia Woolf Society's Misquotations and Misattributions page.
Eavan Boland, Irish poet, born 24 September 1944, died 27 April 2020, professor of English at Stanford from 1996, author of A Journey With Two Maps (2011).
